name: Goal Zero Lighthouse 600
summary: A 600-lumen rechargeable lantern with a dimmer dial, one-side mode, hand crank and USB output; the main-room light for a household outage kit.
verdict:
The Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 is the lantern to put at the center of a household outage kit. It lights a main room through a multi-day outage, with a hand crank and a USB output as useful extras.

**Headroom is the point.** Goal Zero rates it at up to 600 lumens, more than a living room needs. Run it at a third of maximum, about 200 lumens, and it lights the room comfortably while the battery lasts for evenings rather than hours. LED lantern [run time](/glossary/run-time/) scales roughly with brightness, so halving output roughly doubles how long it lasts.

**Two ways to save power.** The dimmer is a dial, not a few fixed steps, so you can set exactly the light you need. You can also light both sides or just one, which halves the drain when the lantern sits against a wall. Folding legs and a hanging handle let you put it where light spreads best.

**Several ways to keep it going.** It recharges over USB from a wall adapter, a car, a power bank or a solar panel such as the [Goal Zero Nomad 20](/gear/goal-zero-nomad-20/). A fold-out hand crank gives emergency light if every battery in the house is flat, though cranking is a trickle, not a recharge. A USB output can top up a phone in a pinch, at the cost of light later.

Owners praise the brightness, the dimmer and the build. The main complaints are the bulk compared with pocket lanterns and how much cranking it takes for a little light. It is the top pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; for warmer light, see the [BioLite AlpenGlow 500](/gear/biolite-alpenglow-500/).

faqs.q: How long does the Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 last on a charge?
faqs.a: It depends on brightness. On low with one side lit, it lasts many hours, enough for several evenings; on the full 600 lumens with both sides lit, it lasts only a few hours. Because LED run time scales roughly with output, dimming to a third of maximum gives you roughly three times the run time.

faqs.q: Can the Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 charge a phone?
faqs.a: Yes, through its USB output, but every bit of phone charge comes out of your light. Use it for an emergency top-up, not as your main phone charger. A separate power bank like the Anker PowerCore 10000 is a better way to keep phones going, and it leaves the lantern’s battery for light.

name: BioLite AlpenGlow 500
summary: A 500-lumen rechargeable lantern with warm white and candle-flicker modes, a 6,400mAh battery and USB output; the most pleasant light for long outage evenings.
verdict:
The BioLite AlpenGlow 500 is the most pleasant lantern to spend an evening with. Choose it over the Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 if light quality matters more to you than a hand crank.

**Warm light makes a dark house feel normal.** BioLite rates it at up to 500 lumens, but its strength is the quality of light at lower settings. A warm white mode and a candle-flicker mode give a room the feel of a lamp rather than a work light, and the frosted body spreads light evenly without glare. A moderate setting lights a living room, which is also where [run time](/glossary/run-time/) is best.

**A big battery for its size.** BioLite lists a 6,400mAh built-in battery, roughly 24Wh. That powers long evenings at low and moderate settings, and the USB output can share some of it with a phone. Every phone top-up comes out of tomorrow night's light, so use it sparingly.

**Plan how you will recharge it.** There is no crank and no solar panel. In a long outage, recharge it over USB from a power bank like the [Anker 737](/gear/anker-737-power-bank/), a USB solar panel or a power station. The IPX4 rating covers rain and splashes, so it can sit on a porch or picnic table.

Owners love the warm light and the shake-to-change color modes, which are a hit with kids. The main complaints are the price and the lack of a crank for worst-case use. It is the ambient-light pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; compare it with the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/).

faqs.a: No. It recharges only over USB, so in a long outage you need another power source: a power bank, a USB solar panel or a power station. Its 6,400mAh battery lasts many evenings at low and moderate settings, so an occasional top-up from a large bank is often enough to keep it going.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the BioLite AlpenGlow 500 and the Goal Zero Lighthouse 600?
faqs.a: Light quality versus backup power. The AlpenGlow has warm white and candle-flicker modes and a frosted body that feels like a lamp. The Lighthouse 600 is brighter, at up to 600 lumens, and adds a hand crank for worst-case use. Both recharge over USB and both can top up a phone.

name: Coleman 400 Lumen LED Lantern
amazonQuery: Coleman 400 Lumen LED Lantern D battery
summary: A rugged 400-lumen camping lantern that runs on D-cell batteries; a dependable closet backup, as long as you store the batteries beside it rather than inside it.
verdict:
The Coleman 400 Lumen LED Lantern is the closet backup that still works after years in storage, as long as you keep the D cells beside it rather than inside it.

**Why D cells still make sense.** A D-cell alkaline battery holds several times the energy of an AA, so a fresh set gives long [run time](/glossary/run-time/) at a moderate setting. When they run low, you swap in new ones in seconds instead of waiting for the power to come back or the sun to come out. On day ten of an outage with no sun, store-bought batteries are the one power source you can count on.

**Enough light for a room.** Coleman rates it at up to 400 lumens, plenty for a kitchen or living room. It is built for camping, so it shrugs off rough handling, and Coleman lists it as water resistant for use outdoors.

**The storage rule.** Alkaline cells left inside a lantern for years can leak and ruin the contacts. Store the batteries in their packaging next to the lantern, and check them when you test your smoke alarms. Buy a spare set, because a lantern without batteries is just a plastic shell.

Owners like the price, the toughness and the simple controls. The main complaints are the weight with batteries installed and the lack of any USB charging. It is the battery pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; for longer run time on D cells, see the [UST 60-Day Duro](/gear/ust-60-day-duro-lantern/), and for a rechargeable option, the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/).

faqs.q: Can I store the Coleman 400 Lumen lantern with the batteries inside?
faqs.a: It is better not to. Alkaline D cells left inside for years can leak and corrode the contacts, which can ruin the lantern. Store the batteries in their original packaging next to the lantern, check them once or twice a year, and install them only when you need light or test the lantern.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Coleman 400 Lumen lantern and a rechargeable lantern?
faqs.a: The power source. The Coleman runs on D-cell batteries you can swap in seconds, which works on day ten of an outage with no sun or grid. A rechargeable lantern like the Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 needs USB power to recharge, but it saves buying batteries and adds a phone-charging output.

name: LuminAID PackLite Max 2-in-1
summary: An inflatable 150-lumen solar lantern with a 2,000mAh battery, USB charging and phone top-up; packs flat, floats and keeps working through a week-long grid-down outage.
verdict:
The LuminAID PackLite Max 2-in-1 is the light most likely to still be working at the end of a week-long grid-down outage, as long as you can put it in direct sun.

**Self-charging and flat-packing.** LuminAID started out making inflatable solar lights for disaster relief. The PackLite Max packs flat to about the thickness of a paperback, inflates into a soft lantern that spreads light well, and recharges from the solar panel on top or over USB. That makes it ideal for a go-bag, a glovebox or a drawer.

**The numbers.** LuminAID rates it at up to 150 lumens, enough for a bedroom or a tent but not a main room, with a 2,000mAh battery and up to 50 hours of [run time](/glossary/run-time/) on low. The 2-in-1 version can also add a small charge to a phone, at the cost of light later.

**Solar needs real sun.** Plan on a full day of direct sun for a good recharge; a cloudy windowsill will not do it. In a long outage, set it outside each morning and bring it in at dusk. The IP67 rating and the fact that it floats matter after a flood or hurricane, when a regular lantern might be ruined.

Owners like that it is always ready and the soft, even light. The main complaints are the dim maximum output and an inflatable body that feels less sturdy than a hard lantern. It is the solar pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; for a smaller solar light, see the [Goal Zero Crush Light](/gear/goal-zero-crush-light/), and for a main room, the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/).

faqs.q: How long does the LuminAID PackLite Max take to charge in the sun?
faqs.a: Plan on a full day of direct sun for a good recharge. Clouds, shade and window glass all slow it sharply. Over USB it charges much faster, so top it up from a wall outlet or power bank while you still have power, and rely on solar to keep it going once the outage drags on.

faqs.q: Is the LuminAID PackLite Max waterproof?
faqs.a: Yes. LuminAID rates it IP67, which covers dust and immersion in water, and it floats. That makes it a good light for hurricane and flood kits, boats and camping. Let it dry fully before you deflate and store it, so moisture is not trapped in the folds for months.

name: Goal Zero Lighthouse Micro Flash
amazonQuery: Goal Zero Lighthouse Micro Flash lantern
summary: A pocket-sized 150-lumen USB-rechargeable lantern and flashlight; cheap enough to give one to every person in the house and keep the big lantern for the main room.
verdict:
The Goal Zero Lighthouse Micro Flash is an inexpensive personal light. Give one to every member of the household and keep the big lantern for the main room.

**Small but useful.** It is a cylinder about the size of a roll of coins that works as both a lantern and a flashlight. Goal Zero rates it at up to 150 lumens, plenty for a bedroom, a bathroom or a walk to the garage. A loop lets you hang it from a door handle or a tent, so nobody fumbles for a phone at 3 a.m.

**One light per person solves the real problem.** The most common outage frustration is one good light and several people who need it. At this size and price you can put one in every bedroom and still afford a main lantern like the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/). Keep them all on the same twice-a-year recharge schedule as the rest of the kit, since built-in batteries slowly drain in storage.

**Know what it is not.** There is no phone-charging output on the Micro Flash, and the battery is built in, so you cannot swap cells when it runs flat. Recharge it over USB from a wall adapter, a car, a power bank like the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) or a USB solar panel. If you want a USB output, Goal Zero sells the Lighthouse Micro Charge.

Owners like the size, the dual lantern and flashlight modes, and the price. The main complaint is that it is too small to light a large room. It is the small-lantern pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; for a solar personal light, see the [Goal Zero Crush Light](/gear/goal-zero-crush-light/).

name: Black Diamond Moji
summary: A palm-sized hanging lantern with a frosted globe, sold in AAA and rechargeable versions; soft, glare-free light for kids’ rooms, bathrooms and hallways.
verdict:
The Black Diamond Moji is a cheap, cheerful personal lantern for children, bathrooms and hallways, not the main room.

**Soft light where you need it.** The Moji is a palm-sized lantern with a frosted globe that turns a small amount of light into an even glow. That is exactly what a child's bedroom or a bathroom needs in an outage, and it is easier on sleepy eyes than a bright lantern. A built-in hook hangs it from a door, a closet rod or a tent loop.

**Pick your version.** Black Diamond sells it in several versions: the standard Moji runs on three AAA batteries, and rechargeable versions charge over USB. Brightness and [run time](/glossary/run-time/) vary between them, so read the listing to see which you are getting. If you choose the AAA version, standardize on the same cells as your headlamps, like the [Black Diamond Spot 400](/gear/black-diamond-spot-400-headlamp/), and keep spares in the kit.

**Kid-proof enough.** It survives being dropped by a seven-year-old, and Black Diamond rates it IPX4 for splashes, so a trip outside in light rain is fine. It is not bright enough to light a kitchen for cooking or a basement for checking a sump pump, and it does not try to be.

Owners like the size, the soft light and how easy it is for kids to use. The main complaints are the low maximum output and AAA cells draining quickly on high. It is the kids pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; for a room light, see the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/).

name: Black Diamond Spot 400
summary: A 400-lumen AAA headlamp with an IPX8 waterproof rating, red night mode and dimming; the hands-free light every adult in the house should have for outages.
verdict:
The Black Diamond Spot 400 is the headlamp every adult in the house should have, a proven and well-built default for working in the dark.

**Hands-free is the point.** A headlamp is the light you wish you had the first time you carry a bucket, reset a breaker or check the basement while holding a phone in your mouth. The Spot 400 puts light where you look and leaves both hands free, which no lantern can do.

**The spec sheet.** Black Diamond rates it at up to 400 lumens on three AAA batteries, with an IPX8 waterproof rating, so a trip outside to check storm damage in a downpour will not hurt it. A red night-vision mode lets you move around without waking anyone, dimming trades brightness for [run time](/glossary/run-time/), and PowerTap lets you jump between full and dimmed output with a tap on the housing.

**AAA or rechargeable.** The AAA version is best for long outages because you can swap cells in seconds; keep a spare set in the kit and standardize on AAA with lights like the [Black Diamond Moji](/gear/black-diamond-moji/). Black Diamond also sells the rechargeable Spot 400-R if you prefer to charge over USB from a power bank.

Owners praise the brightness, the build and the waterproofing. The common complaints are a button layout that takes practice and AAA cells draining quickly on full power. It is a focused beam, not a room light, so pair it with a lantern like the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/). It is the headlamp pick in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup.

faqs.a: Yes. Black Diamond rates it IPX8, the top rating on the standard IPX water scale, which covers heavy rain and submersion. That makes it a safe choice for checking storm damage, clearing a drain or working outside in a downpour during an outage. Dry the battery compartment after a soaking.

faqs.q: Should I buy the Spot 400 or the rechargeable Spot 400-R?
faqs.a: For an outage kit, the AAA Spot 400. You can swap in fresh AAA cells in seconds, which matters on day five with no power. The Spot 400-R charges over USB, which is cheaper and more convenient for regular use, but it depends on a charged power bank or outlet when the grid is down.

name: Goal Zero Crush Light
amazonQuery: Goal Zero Crush Light solar lantern
summary: A collapsible 60-lumen solar lantern that also charges over USB and runs up to 35 hours on low; a small, always-ready personal light for go-bags and kids’ rooms.
verdict:
The Goal Zero Crush Light is a small collapsible solar lantern for a go-bag, a car kit or a child's bedroom. It is not a room light, but it is one of the easiest lights to keep ready.

**Collapses flat, charges itself.** It squashes down flat for storage and pops up into a lantern. A solar panel on top recharges the built-in battery in direct sun, and a USB port recharges it faster from a wall adapter or a power bank. That combination means it is usually ready when you grab it.

**The numbers.** Goal Zero rates it at up to 60 lumens, enough for a bathroom, a tent or reading, and up to 35 hours of [run time](/glossary/run-time/) on low, which can stretch across several nights of careful use. On high, it drains much faster.

**Where it fits.** Think of it as a personal light, like the [Goal Zero Lighthouse Micro Flash](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-micro-flash/), but with solar charging. Next to the [LuminAID PackLite Max](/gear/luminaid-packlite-max/), it is smaller and dimmer; the PackLite is rated at up to 150 lumens and can top up a phone. For a main room, you still want a lantern like the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/).

Owners like the low price, the collapsible design and solar charging that simply works. The main complaints are the dim maximum output and slow solar charging in weak sun. Compare it with the picks in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup.

name: UST 60-Day Duro LED Lantern
summary: A 1,200-lumen D-cell lantern rated to run up to 60 days on low; bright enough to cook by on high and frugal enough on low to stretch one set of batteries across a long outage.
verdict:
The UST 60-Day Duro is a bright, long-running battery lantern for the closet. It pairs a high maximum output with a low mode built to stretch a set of D cells across weeks of nights.

**The 60-day claim, explained.** UST rates it to run up to 60 days on its low setting. That is continuous low-mode [run time](/glossary/run-time/), and low is a dim glow suited to a night light or hallway, not reading. Use high for tasks and low for all-night light, and one set of fresh D cells covers a long outage.

**Bright when you need it.** At up to 1,200 lumens on high, it outshines every rechargeable lantern in our roundup. That is enough to light a kitchen for cooking or a garage for checking a breaker panel. High drains batteries far faster than low, so treat full output as a tool, not a setting to leave on.

**D cells, with the usual storage rule.** Like the [Coleman 400 Lumen LED Lantern](/gear/coleman-400-lumen-led-lantern/), it runs on alkaline D cells you can swap in seconds, which works on day ten with no sun or grid. Store the batteries outside the lantern to avoid leaks, and keep a spare set. UST rates it IPX4 for splashes and rain.

Owners praise the brightness and the long run time on low. The main complaints are the weight with batteries installed and how dim the low mode is. Compare it with the picks in our [best emergency lantern](/best-emergency-lantern/) roundup; for a rechargeable main lantern, see the [Goal Zero Lighthouse 600](/gear/goal-zero-lighthouse-600/).
